This greatly helped reduce the standard deviation and cause uniform fiber length for glass and carbon fibers.  The compaction zone from V1 had to be re-designed to an expanded compaction unit with 14 roller stations. Figure 22 illustrates the CAD drawings of the redesigned compaction units. The 14-roller compaction has a metal mesh that wraps around the compaction zone. The rollers can be adjusted along their vertical to tailor the tension (increase or decrease) by moving the rollers up or down. The distance between the rollers can also be adjusted. The overall spacing of the rollers enables configuring the compaction zone to provide a high degree of material interaction with the rolls and hence increase the compaction. Figure 23 illustrates the re- designed compaction station per the CAD drawing. Figure 24 is the entire line SMC-V2 at the MDF, ORNL.  The motors were changed from induction to servo motors to make the system very quiet during its operation and provide more precision control to advance the fiber.  The system modules were engineered to feed recycled carbon fiber and/or continuous fiber feed to the conveyor – this is explained in the hybrid SMC section.  The doctor boxes were also redesigned to enable precision adjustment of the gap where the resin is poured and forms a film at the gap. Adjustable screws were added to enable increase/decrease of the gap to form resins of different film thickness(es).  The GUI was updated to meter, mix and dispense the fibers as they are layed down.  The front end of the SMC line has been reworked to be more modular. Owens corning glass fiber, Mafic basalt fiber, and a range of TCF carbon fibers were studied for their cut quality. The TCF is broadly from Kaltex and Montefibre precursor. The fibers are either epoxy or urethane sized. One of the fiber lots is hydrosized using a water-based polymer. Table 3 summarizes the fiber types studied for their SMC cut quality.
